This second vignette is a technical tour of the rtists package: how the pieces
fit together, the exact algorithms behind `prune()` and `fatten()`, how the
browser widget renders the data, and how rtists compares with the alternatives
(`rgl`, `plotly`, or a future Rust rewrite). Read the
["Getting started" vignette](rtists.html) first if you have not used the package
before. This one answers *how it works*, not *how to call it*.

---

## Package architecture

`rtists` wraps `fiber` tractography objects (streamline, bundle, bundle_set)
into interactive 3-D visualisations. The whole package in one sentence:

> A fiber object flows through an internal long-data-frame pipeline into one of
> two htmlwidget backends, a three.js renderer (default) or a `plotly`
> `scatter3d` plot.

The dependency shape is deliberately light:

| Concern | Package |
|---|---|
| Data model | `fiber` (S7 classes) |
| Object system | `S7` |
| Widget plumbing | `htmlwidgets` |
| JSON / serialisation | `jsonlite` |
| Console messaging | `cli` |
| 3-D renderer | vendored three.js r186 (ESM) |
| Optional second renderer | `plotly` (Suggests, opt-in) |

There is no compiled code and no `SystemRequirements`, which is central to the
package's CRAN-clean posture. The 3-D rendering happens entirely in the browser
via vendored JavaScript.

### The public surface

The exported API is small:

- `plot3d()`: an S7 generic with methods for the three fiber classes. Returns an
  htmlwidget.
- `prune()`: an S7 generic that thins an overlapping bundle to a spread-out
  subset whose tubes do not touch.
- `fatten()`: an S7 generic that attaches a visible tube radius to streamlines
  that carry none.

Everything else is internal. Because the fiber classes are namespaced
(`fiber::streamline` and so on), plain S3 dispatch breaks on them, so rtists
uses **S7 generics** with methods declared on the S7 classes directly. The
per-class data-frame conversion helpers (`.streamline_to_df`, `.bundle_to_df`,
`.bundle_set_to_df`) are plain internal functions rather than S3/S7 methods,
precisely because the class names carry a `::` prefix that S3 dispatch cannot
match.

---

## The data pipeline

Whatever the input class, `plot3d()` funnels the object through the same path:

```
fiber object
   └─ .streamline_to_df / .bundle_to_df / .bundle_set_to_df
        └─ long data frame (one row per point, metadata as extra columns)
             └─ .rbind_union (align frames to the union of columns, NA fill)
                  └─ resolved data frame
                       └─ .plot3d_threejs  ──► three.js htmlwidget
                       └─ .plot3d_impl     ──► plotly htmlwidget
```

### Long-form data frame

Each streamline becomes a block of rows with the columns `StreamlineId`,
`PointId`, `X`, `Y`, `Z`, plus one column per metadata key. A streamline with
per-point `FA` and per-streamline `mean_FA` becomes:

```{r}
#| label: df-shape
pts <- matrix(c(0,0,0, 1,2,1, 2,3,3), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE,
              dimnames = list(NULL, c("X","Y","Z")))
sl  <- streamline(pts, point_data = list(FA = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8)),
                  streamline_data = list(mean_FA = 0.5))
d   <- rtists:::.streamline_to_df(sl, streamline_id = 1L)
d
```

Per-streamline scalars are broadcast to every point of their streamline, so the
long frame is uniformly point-based. This flat shape is what makes the widget
backend straightforward: the renderer only ever consumes points, colours, and
an optional per-point radius.

### Aligning heterogenous objects

A single streamlines' frame has as many columns as it has metadata keys. When
several streamlines (or bundles, or bundle sets) carry different keys,
`.rbind_union` aligns them to the **union** of all columns, filling the missing
cells with `NA`. Those `NA` cells never reach the renderer as geometry; they are
metadata only, and the widget skips missing values in the tooltip and the
legend panel.

---

## Backend routing

The default backend is **three.js**. The choice is made inside each S7 method by
`match.arg(backend)` after building the shared data frame, so the two backends
consume the exact same resolved frame. Only the three.js backend understands
`radius`, `bg`, and `tooltip`; the `plotly` backend ignores those and instead
forwards any `...` arguments to `plotly::layout()` (the only backend that honours
a custom `...`).

---

## The three.js backend

The three.js backend lives in `R/backend-threejs.R`, which builds the widget
payload, and in `inst/htmlwidgets/lib/threejs/rtists-render.js`, which renders
it.

### Payload and binary encoding

A naive widget would send coordinates as JSON floating-point numbers
(17 significant digits each). For even a 100k-point bundle that bloats the
widget JSON enormously. rtists instead packs numerical buffers as **raw binary
little-endian** and lets `htmlwidgets` base64-encode the byte strings, giving
compact payloads:

| Field | Type | Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| `positions` | Float32 xyz (3 per point) | `writeBin(pos, raw(), size = 4L)` -> base64 |
| `colors` | Uint8 RGB (3 per point) | `as.raw(pmin(255L, round(colors * 255)))` -> base64 |
| `radii` (tube mode) | Float32 (1 per point) | `writeBin(..., size = 4L)` -> base64 |
| `ramp` (legend) | Uint8 3 x 256 | raw -> base64 |

The JS side decodes them back with `atob` and typed-array views
(`b64ToF32`, `b64ToU8F32`). Positions and radii cross the wire at **Float32**
precision; colours cross at 8-bit channels, which is exactly what the canvas
samples anyway.

### Two render paths

The widget branches on a `mode` field set on the R side.

**line2 mode (default).** A single `LineSegments2` mesh with a
`LineMaterial({ worldUnits: true, vertexColors: true, linewidth })`. Interleaved
segment buffers `[start, end]` per segment, with per-segment start/end colours.
Because everything is one draw call, this path scales to large bundles and is
the default. Constant world-space width via the `linewidth` uniform. The classic
three.js `resolution` footgun (an unset `resolution` uniform producing `NaN`
aspect in the shader) is self-healed in r186 by `LineSegmentsGeometry`'s
`onBeforeRender` hook, so no manual handling is needed.

**tube mode.** One `TubeGeometry` per streamline, built at **unit radius** around
a `CatmullRomCurve3`, then every ring of vertices is displaced radially by that
streamline's per-point radius, and a per-vertex `color` attribute supplies the
fill. Because the tube is built at unit radius and displaced, a single geometry
can represent a radius that varies along the streamline. Object-level depth
sorting gives transparent tubes: each tube is its own mesh with
`transparent: true` and `depthWrite: false`, so transparent tubes compose
correctly instead of flickering.

### The radius knob in detail

`rtists` never decides a radius for you beyond what you ask for, and it never
shrinks tubes or hides streamlines to dodge overlap. Overlap is the generator's
business, not rtists's. The `radius` argument resolves through a small set of
helpers:

1. `.df_radius_from_data(df)` recovers a radius carried on the object itself: a
   `radius` column in the resolved frame. If the radius is constant within each
   streamline it returns a per-streamline vector; otherwise a per-point vector;
   `NULL` when no usable positive radius exists.
2. `.threejs_radius(radius, df)` resolves the explicit `radius` argument into a
   `mode` and per-point radii. It accepts:
   - `NULL` / `0`: fast `line2` (either "use the object's own radius" or "plain
     thin lines").
   - a positive scalar: constant-radius tubes.
   - a per-streamline vector (length == number of streamlines).
   - a per-point vector (length == total number of points).

   Positivity is validated; this echoes the "radial displacement of a unit
   tube" design, where the most general form (per-point) is the same code path
   as a scalar.

### Hovering, tooltips, and the legend panel

The widget ships a small in-scene DOM tooltip. On pointer move it raycasts the
mesh, maps the hit back to a packed point index, and renders the pinned bundle
name and coordinates plus the toggleable attribute columns. Line2 mode maps a
raycast segment index to a point via a `segToPoint` index; tube mode finds the
nearest point within the hit streamline.

A separate legend panel (from `.df_legend_meta`) lets the user remap aesthetics
live without re-framing the camera: colour by bundle or any attribute, radius
by any numeric attribute (tube mode), and per-bundle or per-streamline
visibility. The R side ships a 3 x 256 Uint8 colour ramp plus per-streamline
and per-point attribute buffers; the JS side rebuilds the mesh in place from
decoded buffers. Anything missing (a `NULL`/`NaN` value) is painted a
distinct grey, never dropped silently.

---

## `prune()` and `fatten()`: the algorithms

`plot3d()` renders whatever it is given. For bundles of *thin* streamlines that
carry no radius, the picture can be a tangle of overlapping lines. `prune()` and
`fatten()` are companion utilities that turn a dense bundle into a legible one.

### `prune()`: keep a non-overlapping spread

`prune(x, radius, overlap_margin = 1, max_iter = Inf)` returns a subset whose
tubes of the given radius do not overlap. The core is `.prune_indices(polys,
radius, overlap_margin, max_iter)`:

1. **Required separation**: `req = 2 * radius * overlap_margin` (tube diameter,
   scaled by the margin). Two streamlines count as "not overlapping" when their
   `.min_sep_two` (closest approach between the two polyline geometries) is at
   least `req`.
2. **Greedy, deterministic selection**, starting from an empty kept set:
   - if nothing is kept yet, consider the remaining streamlines in raw index
     order;
   - otherwise, among the remaining streamlines, choose **farthest-first**: the
     one whose gap to the kept set (`.streamline_cover_gap`) is largest, ties
     broken by index, and keep the first one whose tube does not overlap any
     kept tube (every `.min_sep_two` at least `req`).
3. **Stop** as soon as every remaining streamline is "covered"
   (`.streamline_cover_gap <= radius`, meaning the kept tubes already span the
   whole hull at the given radius), or when no remaining streamline has a
   non-overlapping candidate.

The result is `sort(keep)`: a deterministic, reproducible spread. Beyond the
index tie-break the outcome does not depend on input order, so the same bundle
prunes the same way every time.

### `fatten()`: give thin streamlines a visible radius

`fatten(x, visibility = NULL, ...)` attaches a constant per-streamline `radius`
so that radius-less streamlines render as tubes instead of hairline lines. It
chooses the radius from the geometry:

- `.fatten_step(polys)`: the median intra-streamline sampling step (median
  distance between consecutive points along a streamline).
- `.fatten_dmin(polys)`: the **minimum** distance between any two streamlines.
- `.fatten_floor(polys, visibility)`: the visible-radius floor. Either a
  user-supplied `visibility` (validated to a single positive number), or the
  median step as a sensible default.

The bundle method decides between two regimes on how the streamlines sit
relative to one another, with `f` the floor and `dmin` the closest approach:

- **Sparse** (`dmin / 2 >= f`): streamlines are far enough apart that tubes of
  radius `dmin / 2` *just touch*. Everything is kept, at that radius: the
  visually fullest picture with no overlap.
- **Dense** (`dmin / 2 < f`): streamlines overlap at any visible radius, so
  `fatten()` falls back to pruning: the radius is $r = f$ (the floor) and
  `kept` is the `.prune_indices(polys, f, 1)` subset, giving non-overlapping tubes at the
  visible floor.

The `bundle_set` method simply applies `fatten()` to each bundle in turn and
drops any that become empty.

#### Where the radius lands

A subtle and important detail: `fatten()` does **not** attach the radius to each
nested streamline. It calls

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fiber::bundle(kept, streamline_data = list(radius = rep(r, length(kept))))
```

`fiber::bundle()` hoists per-streamline metadata to the bundle-level
`@streamline_data` slot (a per-streamline vector of length *S*), rather than
nesting it inside each streamline. This is the same slot `plot3d()` reads back
via `.df_radius_from_data()`, so the fattened radius flows straight through the
pipeline. This is why a bundle that `fatten()` returns renders as tubes on a
bare `plot3d(x)` call with no `radius` argument: the radius now lives in the
object's data.

The `fatten()` method for a single streamline always applies the visibility
floor (there is nothing to prune), and the empty-bundle case is handled
explicitly as `fiber::bundle(list())`.

---

## Assessment: three.js vs rgl vs plotly vs Rust

The comparison that motivated the three.js choice, and the question of whether
to keep the `plotly` backend or one day move the renderer to native code.

### three.js (the chosen end state)

**Strengths.** A single `LineSegments2` draw call plus per-vertex colour buffers
scales to very large bundles. Real world-space tube geometry (`TubeGeometry` +
radial displacement) gives genuine 3-D thickness and Phong flat shading, which
rgl gives but `plotly` cannot. Object-level depth-sorted transparency renders
overlapping transparent tubes correctly. It stays a self-contained inline
htmlwidget with **no `SystemRequirements`** and no compiled code, preserving the
CRAN-clean posture.

**Costs.** The plotting code is JavaScript. Engineering it (payload encoding,
the ESM loading trick, the two render paths, hover + legend) was a one-time
effort of a few hundred lines of JS. The off-the-shelf `rthreejs` package is a
thin wrapper and not suited to this level of control, so rtists vendors three.js
directly.

### rgl (the neuroimaging standard) -- why it loses

`rgl` offers true OpenGL lighting and the interactive `rglwidget()`, and it is
the usual tool in tractography. But adopting it would mean:

- adding `SystemRequirements` (GLEW/GLU/GL on Linux, X on some systems), which
  broke the "no SystemRequirements" CRAN posture that motivated this design;
- `lines3d()` issues one GL draw call per line, which is slow for huge bundles
  compared to a single `LineSegments` draw call;
- continuous per-point colour on a single line requires splitting it into per
  segment sub-lines to vary the colour;
- the widget still opens a GL context and needs a virtual framebuffer in
  headless CI.

The three.js renderer *can* approach rgl's "cinematic" look (tubes, lighting,
depth-sorted transparency) without any of those costs.

### plotly (kept, but as a deliberate opt-in)

The two backends were assessed again after the r186 upgrade. `plotly` renders
flat, screen-space line strips: no real thickness, no lighting, no depth-sorted
transparency. Before r186 it had a credible payoff (line width, interactivity)
that the upgrade removed, so its original justification is gone. rtists keeps
it for two specific reasons:

1. it is the **only** backend that honours `...`, forwarding to
   `plotly::layout()` (handy for titles and scene tweaks);
2. it is a **resilient second renderer** if WebGL is unavailable.

It is therefore exposed as `backend = "plotly"`, an explicit opt-in rather than
a default.

### Moving to Rust (the scale ceiling)

The binding constraint for very large bundles is *not* the renderer. Per the
whole-brain benchmark (5 M points), both htmlwidget backends are limited by
**JSON text encoding** of the payload: roughly 278 MB of binary floats become
around 444 MB of JSON and over a gigabyte of HTML, taking 4-52 s just to
serialise. At 10^5 points everything is instant; at 10^6 to 10^7 points a saved
inline widget becomes impractical for either backend, because both are
htmlwidgets sharing the same serialisation ceiling.

The escape that a Rust implementation would offer is a **local server
architecture**: transfer the same binary floats over a WebSocket (or WASM),
avoiding JSON text entirely. But rtists is deliberately a *static, self-contained
htmlwidget*: embeddable, shareable, openable from a saved `.html`. A streaming
server would invert that contract (the widget becomes a client of a running
local process) and add a compiled server dependency, exactly what the package
avoids. That reassessment concluded **no WebSocket/streaming backend**: it
would only pay off at a scale that is beyond the htmlwidget's practical range
regardless of transport, and it sacrifices the self-contained artifact. If
whole-brain self-contained output is ever truly needed at 10^6+ points, the path
is a genuinely binary-embedded artifact (a base64 blob of a `Float32Array`
fetched within one HTML file), not a server that rtists must ship.

### Bottom line

For the overwhelming majority of tractography work (single tracts up to whole
bundles, tens to hundreds of thousands of points), the three.js htmlwidget is
the right shape: no native dependencies, real 3-D tubes and transparency, and a
fast single-draw-call default. The `plotly` backend stays as an opt-in,
`...`-honouring fallback. A Rust local-server rewrite would only be justified
by the 10^6-point scale ceiling, and even then it fights the htmlwidget's core
promise of a self-contained, shareable artifact.
